findings.claim: 29 practice questions across all eleven lessons are typed '8 marks - Explain Why'; several carry no stimulus bullets.
findings.truth: The British depth study booklet sets only three forms: 'Describe two features of...' (4), 'Explain why...' (12, with two stimulus bullets and 'You must also use information of your own'), and a choice of '‘Statement.’ How far do you agree?' (16) - 32 marks in all. All 29 retyped to 12 marks, band ladders rebuilt to the 12-mark standard, and the eleven questions that had no stimulus given two bullets.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/history-1HI0.md assessment section (Paper 2 booklet B = 32 marks; SPaG sits on Paper 1 and Paper 3 only, 8 SPaG marks in the whole qualification)

findings.claim: Exam tips in L1, L3, L4, L6, L9, L10 and L11 promise SPaG marks ('for top-band SPaG', 'the 4 SPaG marks reward...', 'avoidance of medieval terminology caps SPaG at the threshold band').
findings.truth: Paper 2 carries no marks for spelling, punctuation and grammar. The qualification's 8 SPaG marks are on Paper 1 and on Paper 3 question 3(d). Every SPaG promise replaced with the true statement.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/history-1HI0.md assessment section (Paper 2 booklet B = 32 marks; SPaG sits on Paper 1 and Paper 3 only, 8 SPaG marks in the whole qualification)

findings.claim: L9 'examiners want a sequence of distinct, weighted causes'; L11 'examiners reward a substantiated overall verdict'; L1 'the mark scheme rewards clear separation'; L9 generalisations 'always cap responses below the top band'.
findings.truth: Invented exam and mark-scheme claims. Rewritten as plain advice to the student.
findings.evidence: house rule on invented exam claims

findings.claim: L2, L4, L7 and L9 exam tips coach an '8-mark Explain Why question'; L3 sends narrative to 'the 8 and 16-mark questions'.
findings.truth: There is no 8-mark question on this paper. Retariffed to 12 marks.
findings.evidence: specs/edexcel/history-1HI0.md assessment section (Paper 2 booklet B = 32 marks; SPaG sits on Paper 1 and Paper 3 only, 8 SPaG marks in the whole qualification)

findings.claim: 'his elder brothers Henry the Young King and Geoffrey were already dead'.
findings.truth: Geoffrey (b. 1158) was younger than Richard (b. 1157). L5 of this unit correctly calls Geoffrey John's elder brother, so the unit contradicted itself on the succession that Arthur's claim rests on.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Henry II of England' children; internal contradiction with L5

findings.claim: 'Returning from the Holy Land in 1193, Richard appointed Hubert Walter as Archbishop of Canterbury and chief justiciar.'
findings.truth: Richard was a prisoner in Germany throughout 1193 and was not freed until 4 February 1194. Walter was elected archbishop on 29 May 1193 and made chief justiciar about 25 December 1193, at the captive king's direction.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Hubert Walter'; Wikipedia 'Richard I of England'

findings.claim: 'The king then levied a special tax called the Saladin Tithe his father had begun'; the mark scheme for question 2 lists 'Continuation of the Saladin Tithe'.
findings.truth: Richard did not levy the Saladin Tithe. He spent the treasury his father had already filled with it and raised the rest by selling offices, charters and lands.

findings.claim: Mark scheme: Richard 'trusted him with the Great Seal'.
findings.truth: Hubert Walter was never Chancellor under Richard; John appointed him Chancellor on 27 May 1199. Under Richard he held the justiciarship.

findings.claim: Match set labels John 'Untrusted regent figure who tried to seize power'.
findings.truth: John held no regency. Richard's government was in the hands of the justiciars; John's 1191-94 attempt was rebellion, not regency.
findings.evidence: spec B2 key topic 1.3 (government in Richard's absence)

findings.claim: 'the deathbed reconciliation at Chinon left him as the obvious heir'.
findings.truth: The peace was made at Ballan (the treaty of Azay-le-Rideau) on 4 July 1189; Henry II was then carried to Chinon, where he died on 6 July. The compression is defensible for GCSE, so no edit.

findings.claim: 'Henry II and Philip II ... took the Cross at Gisors on 21 January 1188. Richard, then count of Poitou, took it later that year. He was the first ruler in north-western Europe to swear the crusading vow.'
findings.truth: Richard took the Cross at Tours in November 1187, before his father and before Gisors - which is what makes the next sentence true. As written the two sentences contradict each other.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Richard I of England' ('Richard took the cross as Count of Poitou in 1187', at Tours)

findings.claim: The English fleet 'that left in 1190' is said to have 'helped storm a small Moorish fortress at Silves in 1189'.
findings.truth: Silves was besieged 21 July - 3 September 1189 by a separate northern crusader fleet that left Bremen in April 1189 (Germans, Danes, Frisians, Flemings and some English), not by the Angevin fleet of 1190.

findings.claim: Richard 'married Berengaria of Navarre' in the Sicily sentence, before the conquest of Cyprus.
findings.truth: Richard married Berengaria at Limassol in Cyprus in May 1191, not in Sicily.

findings.claim: 'The fall of the Holy City triggered Pope Gregory VIII's call for a Third Crusade in his bull Audita tremendi.'
findings.truth: Audita tremendi was issued on 29 October 1187 in response to the defeat at Hattin; news of Jerusalem's fall on 2 October had barely had time to reach Rome. The textbook shorthand is standard, so no edit.

findings.claim: Richard 'pushed inland twice in late 1191 and early 1192 - up the road to Beit Nuba'.
findings.truth: The two advances to Beit Nuba were the winter of 1191-92 (retreat 13 January 1192) and June 1192 (retreat 4 July 1192).

findings.claim: Mark scheme: Henry VI 'was at odds with Richard over the rival Welf candidate Henry the Lion (Richard's brother-in-law)'.
findings.truth: Henry the Lion was never a candidate for the imperial throne; his son Otto was elected only in 1198. Henry VI's hostility rested on Richard's alliance with the Welfs and with Tancred of Sicily.

findings.claim: 'The first instalment was paid at Speyer in February 1194 and Richard was released' (repeated in the knowledge-check match set as 'Richard released at Speyer').
findings.truth: The date, 4 February 1194, is secure. The place is not: most modern accounts give Mainz for the release, and Speyer for the handover to Henry VI in March 1193, but Wikipedia's 'Henry VI' article says Speyer for 1194. Two options: change both mentions to Mainz, or drop the place and keep only 'February 1194'. Recommend dropping the place - it is not examinable and the sources disagree.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Richard I of England' (date only); Wikipedia 'Henry VI, Holy Roman Emperor' (Speyer)

findings.claim: 'The most credible contemporary account - the Margam Annals - reports that on 3 April 1203 a drunken John personally killed his nephew'.
findings.truth: The Margam annals are the fullest account of Arthur's death, but their reliability is debated (the abbey had de Braose patronage). 'Most credible' presents a historiographical judgement as fact; changed to 'the fullest'.
findings.evidence: standard historiography of Arthur of Brittany

findings.claim: Mirebeau mark scheme: 'experienced English and Norman household knights led by William Marshal and other senior commanders'.
findings.truth: The commander who brought John to Mirebeau was William des Roches, seneschal of Anjou, whose later defection over Arthur was decisive. William Marshal was not the commander there.

findings.claim: 'Roger of Wendover called him ‘cruel to all men’'.
findings.truth: The Matthew Paris quotation in the same sentence checks out. The Wendover phrase could not be verified in any consulted source. Not corrected, because the true wording was not found; if Tom cannot place it, replace with an unattributed paraphrase.
findings.evidence: no source found on Wikipedia 'John, King of England' or 'Roger of Wendover'

findings.claim: Chateau Gaillard stood 'twenty-five miles downstream from Rouen'.
findings.truth: It stands between Paris and Rouen, i.e. 25 miles UPSTREAM of Rouen. The lesson's own mark scheme for question 5 already says 'upstream'.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Chateau Gaillard' (40 km from Rouen, on the Seine between Paris and Rouen)

findings.claim: The siege of Chateau Gaillard 'began in August 1203' (four places in the lesson, plus a flashcard answer), yet the same lesson says the garrison 'held out for six months' and the mark scheme says 'around six months'.
findings.truth: The siege ran from September 1203 to 6 March 1204 - which is the six months the lesson claims. August 1203 is when Philip took the town and island of Les Andelys.

findings.claim: 'around 200 knights and sergeants under Roger de Lacy'.
findings.truth: Wikipedia gives 20 knights and 120 other soldiers; other accounts say about 300 with refugees. The figure is soft in the sources, so no edit.

findings.claim: 'By 1214 the rate was £3 per knight's fee.'
findings.truth: The 1214 scutage was three MARKS per knight's fee (a mark is two-thirds of a pound). L9 of this unit states it correctly, so the unit contradicted itself on the figure that explains the Northerners' refusal.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Scutage' ('in 1214, John demanded three marks'); internal contradiction with L9

findings.claim: 'John demanded reliefs of £1,000, £5,000, even (in the case of William fitz Alan) £7,000' - repeated in the conclusion, the exam tip, two mark schemes and a flashcard answer.
findings.truth: L9 carries the documented figures: 7,000 marks from John de Lacy and 10,000 marks from William fitz Alan. L7 gave the wrong man for the 7,000 and converted marks into pounds throughout.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction with L9; John de Lacy's 7,000-mark relief of 1213 is the standard example

findings.claim: The 1207 thirteenth was 'the first English tax assessed on personal wealth as a whole, rather than on land or feudal status' (repeated in a mark scheme).
findings.truth: The Saladin Tithe of 1188 and the ransom quarter of 1193-94 had already taxed income and moveables - as this unit says in L2 and L4. What was new in 1207 was a tax of this kind for the king's own war rather than for a crusade or a ransom.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction with L2 and L4

findings.claim: Innocent III 'would shortly launch the Fourth Crusade' - written of the years 1205-07.
findings.truth: The Fourth Crusade was called in 1198 and ended with the sack of Constantinople in 1204, before the Canterbury dispute described here.

findings.claim: 'in 1215 he produced a copy of Henry I's coronation charter as a model for what would become Magna Carta'.
findings.truth: Langton read out Henry I's charter of liberties at a council of churchmen and barons on 25 August 1213.

findings.claim: The rebels mustered 'at Northampton, where they formally renounced their oaths of homage on 5 May' (repeated in a mark scheme, a knowledge-check match set and a flashcard).
findings.truth: The renunciation of homage on 5 May 1215 is usually placed at Brackley, with the defiance delivered to John at Wallingford; the siege of Northampton began about 12 May. The spec bullet names Northampton, Lincoln and the march on London, and several GCSE textbooks put the diffidatio at Northampton. Options: leave as is (matches the spec's list and the common textbook line), or move the renunciation to Brackley in four places. Recommend leaving it, because the sources a student will meet say Northampton.
findings.evidence: spec B2 key topic 3.2; Wikipedia 'First Barons' War'

findings.claim: 'John executed many of the surrendered defenders, against the chivalric custom of his age' - repeated in four mark-scheme bullets.
findings.truth: John ordered the whole garrison hanged but was talked out of it by his captain Savari de Mauleon, who feared reprisals against royal garrisons. Only one man was hanged - a crossbowman who had served John since childhood. The rest were imprisoned.

findings.claim: The rebel barons at Runnymede were 'recently expelled from London for the day to allow negotiations'.
findings.truth: The rebels held London and rode out from it to Runnymede. Nobody expelled them.

findings.claim: '30 November 1215, after a six-week siege.'
findings.truth: The siege ran from 11 October to 30 November 1215, about seven weeks.

findings.claim: 'Clauses 50 and 51 ordered the dismissal of named foreign captains - including Falkes de Breaute and Engelard de Cigogne.'
findings.truth: Clause 50 names Gerard de Athee's relatives, Engelard de Cigogne among them; Falkes de Breaute is not named, though clause 51 required all foreign knights and mercenaries to leave. The substance is right, so no edit.

findings.claim: 'The chronicler at the abbey of St Albans wrote that the king had ‘hurried like a tempest’.'
findings.truth: The wording could not be traced to Roger of Wendover or any other St Albans text in the sources consulted. Not corrected, because the true wording was not found.

findings.claim: Henry III was 'crowned in Gloucester Cathedral ... by the papal legate Guala Bicchieri' - repeated in the key fact, the conclusion, a knowledge-check stem, a flashcard answer and two mark schemes.
findings.truth: Henry III was crowned by Peter des Roches, Bishop of Winchester, and anointed by the bishops of Worcester and Exeter; Guala Bicchieri presided as legate. The flashcard answer key was therefore wrong.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Henry III of England' ('anointed by Bishops Sylvester of Worcester and Simon of Exeter, and crowned by Peter des Roches')

findings.claim: 'The First Barons' War had been running for fifteen months.'
findings.truth: September 1215 to October 1216 is thirteen months. The lesson's own mark scheme dates the war from September 1215.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction with the same lesson's mark scheme

findings.claim: 'the great seal had reportedly been lost in the Wash, and the only major royal asset left in firm loyalist hands was the great castle of Dover'.
findings.truth: What went into the Wash was the baggage train and the regalia - as the lesson itself says two paragraphs later ('the lost regalia'). And the next paragraph names four loyalist castles (Dover, Windsor, Corfe, Nottingham), so Dover was not the only one.

findings.claim: 'the rebel barons held the great northern castles of Lincoln, York and Carlisle'.
findings.truth: Lincoln Castle was held for the king by Nicola de la Haye throughout - which is why the loyalist army had to fight its way into the city in May 1217 to relieve it, as this lesson says later. The rebels held the city, not the castle.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Second Battle of Lincoln'; internal contradiction within the lesson

findings.claim: 'His military leadership at Lincoln in 1217 demonstrated that personal valour still mattered in twelfth-century kingship.'
findings.truth: 1217 is the thirteenth century.

findings.claim: 'the Marshal's twenty-six months as Protector'.
findings.truth: 11 November 1216 to his death on 14 May 1219 is about thirty months.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'William Marshal, 1st Earl of Pembroke' (died 14 May 1219, still regent)

findings.claim: 'on 11 November 1216 a council at Bristol named William Marshal as Protector'.
findings.truth: The date is right. Wikipedia places the naming at Gloucester on 11 November 1216, with the Bristol council issuing the reissued charter dated 12 November. Sources differ on the place, so no edit; if Tom's textbook says Gloucester, change the one word.

findings.claim: 'crowned in Gloucester Cathedral'.
findings.truth: In 1216 the church was St Peter's Abbey, Gloucester; it became a cathedral in 1541. Every GCSE text says Gloucester Cathedral, so no edit.

summary: Eleven lessons checked against Edexcel option B2. Two systemic exam-claim faults ran through the whole unit: 29 practice questions were priced as 8-mark 'Explain why' questions, a form this paper does not set, and seven exam tips promised SPaG marks that Paper 2 does not award. On content, the heaviest errors are the Rochester garrison 'executions' (John was talked out of it; one man hanged), the officiant at Henry III's coronation (Peter des Roches, not the legate), the 1214 scutage priced in pounds instead of marks, the reliefs attributed to the wrong baron, Richard 'returning' in 1193 while he was in fact a prisoner, and Richard taking the Cross after his father rather than before him. Several fixes resolve contradictions the unit already contained between its own lessons.
